articles.title: Why is Morocco celebrating the defeat of a UN resolution on Western Sahara?
articles.summary: Mandate expires for UN mission tasked to monitor 1991 truce and hold a referendum in the disputed territory.
articles.body:
Morocco has welcomed the defeat of a US-drafted resolution which sought to extend the mandate of the UN mission in the disputed Western Sahara.

The mandate of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) expired on Saturday after a veto by Russia, leaving the future of the peacekeeping mission in limbo. In 1991, the UN established MINURSO to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.

Morocco has considered Western Sahara its own territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa which is roughly the size of Britain. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.

So, why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution? What does it mean for the future of the disputed region?

What happened at the UN Security Council?

On Friday, the US, which is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the disputed Western Sahara.

Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 council members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.

The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.

Last October, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution that offered genuine autonomy to Western Sahara. Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs, but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.

The Security Council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.

Speaking after the vote, US ambassador Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026 the veto was used to “preserve the letter R (in the Mission’s name) for referendum”.

He added that Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and added that the status quo is not acceptable.

Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.

“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.

Instead, Russia proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes. But that draft also failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption, receiving two votes in favour, one against and 11 abstentions.

MINURSO’s mission has 155 military personnel and is set to cost $62m in the fiscal year that began in June, according to a UN report. But its mandate expired on Saturday.

How did Morocco and Algeria react to the failure of the UN mission?

Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days and that the Western Sahara issue should now be withdrawn from the Security Council’s consideration. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire.

According to a UN media statement, Morocco’s UN representative also questioned why Algeria’s delegate was giving the Security Council “lectures” on the Western Sahara.

“Let these people [in the Western Sahara] go back to Morocco,” he said, “let them go home”.

Algeria expressed regret on Saturday over the failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate. Its foreign ministry criticised what it described as the US draft’s excessive bias towards Morocco.

According to a UN media statement, Algeria’s delegate to the UN thanked Russia for its draft resolution and all other member nations “who have chosen not to associate themselves” with an egregious injustice and a flagrant attack on “the very foundation of our organisation”.

Algeria’s UN representative noted that the country has been a refuge for hundreds of thousands of Sahrawi people who have been denied their right to self-determination.

The “tragedy being endured by the Sahrawi people has oddly been diluted to the concept of refugee populations”, he added.

Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.

What is the Western Sahara dispute all about?

The Polisario Front, the political and military representative, does not recognise Morocco’s annexation of the territory following Spain’s withdrawal in 1975. It has been seeking a UN-supervised referendum for self-determination.

In 1976, it declared the independent Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.

Decades of fighting drove at least 170,000 Indigenous people into refugee camps in Tindouf in neighbouring Algeria, which backs the Polisario Front.

The Polisario Front signed a UN-brokered ceasefire with Morocco in 1991. It called for a referendum within six months, but it was never held.

Morocco, which retains control of its lucrative phosphate and fishing resources in Western Sahara, claims historic and pre-colonial ties to the land and views the region as an integral part of its territory [“Greater Morocco”].

For decades, the US has provided military and diplomatic support to Morocco. But in 2020, Donald Trump recognised Moroccan sovereignty over the territory during his first term in office. Morocco soon established diplomatic ties with Israel as part of the so-called Abraham Accords.

The region is now the last United Nations-designated “non-self-governing territory” in Africa, where between 100,000 and 140,000 Moroccan military personnel are based.

Low-level fighting has also continued since the Polisario Front said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.

Why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution?

MINURSO was set up to monitor the 1991 ceasefire and hold a referendum in Western Sahara. The expiry of its mandate will likely boost Morocco’s stance on the referendum question, though its autonomy proposal has already been adopted by the UN.

On Saturday, according to a video report by the Reuters news agency, a festive atmosphere prevailed in the streets of El Aaiun, the capital of Western Sahara.

In the central Mechoua Square, dozens of people were wearing melfas, the traditional Sahrawi women’s garments, and long robes known as darra, as they waved Moroccan flags and displayed portraits of Morocco’s King Mohammed VI.

Selim Balouati Lakhloufi, a historian and researcher based in Morocco, said that Morocco is pleased because “diplomatic developments at the United Nations are supporting its strategy regarding the [disputed Western] Sahara”.

“The support of powers such as the United States, France and the United Kingdom for Morocco’s autonomy proposal strengthens its international position and is gradually shifting the debate away from the right to self-determination and the possibility of independence toward a solution based on autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty,” he told Al Jazeera.

What does this mean for the future of the Western Sahara?

The collapse of MINURSO’s mandate could escalate the dispute in the Western Sahara, according to aid organisations.

Oxfam has warned that losing MINURSO’s “monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability”.

Lakhloufi said that the UN mission’s expiry is also unfavourable for Sahrawi independence aspirations.

Regarding the future of the Western Sahara, he said that Morocco will likely continue to consolidate its territorial, economic and administrative control, while the Polisario Front will face greater difficulties in securing international support.

“The proposal for autonomy could end up becoming the main framework for negotiations, pushing independence further and further out of reach,” he added.

articles.title: Bitter spat between Poland’s pro-Europe PM and pro-Trump president erupts
articles.summary: Poland is in the throes of a constitutional crisis as a battle over the future of the country’s highest court ignites another confrontation between the country’s president and prime minister,
articles.body: Poland is in the throes of a constitutional crisis as a battle over the future of the country’s highest court ignites another confrontation between the country’s president and prime minister. The crisis came to a head on Friday when center-left Prime Minister Donald Tusk moved to remake Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, whose chief justice was appointed by the previous government – the far-right Law and Justice party (PiS). The judge, Bogdan Święczkowski, was suspended after refusing to allow a new member of the Tribunal, who had been nominated by Tusk and approved by the Polish parliament, from taking his seat. His deputy was also suspended. The current crisis is the latest and possibly most serious chapter in a long-running dispute over the rule of law in Poland. Tusk’s pro-European Civic Coalition was elected in 2023, after an election campaign in which he promised to restore the Tribunal’s independence. President Karol Nawrocki, who belongs to PiS, was elected separately last year. Poland’s president has little executive power but plays an important constitutional role. Since then, deadlock has become crisis. Nawrocki described Święczkowski’s removal as the chief judge as “a forcible takeover of a constitutional body.” On hearing the news, he abandoned a trip to Africa, ordered his aircraft to turn round and headed straight to the Tribunal. Nawrocki is a vocal supporter of US President Donald Trump, who said in September: “I endorsed him, and now he’s president and he’s doing a fantastic job.” Nawrocki has suggested a new US military base in Poland will be called “Fort Trump”. During its eight years in power – until 2023 - PiS appointed several judges to seats on the Tribunal already filled by the previous government. In 2021, the European Union warned that PiS’ actions posed a “systemic risk to the rule of law in Poland” in undermining the Tribunal’s independence. The European Commission froze $137 billion in EU funding for Poland over concerns about the independence of Polish judges. The PiS-appointed judges remained in place after Tusk was elected and have obstructed his efforts to nominate new judges. Nawrocki has refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by ‌parliament, ‌while Swieczkowski declined to seat the judges chosen by parliament. Last week, the latest judge to be approved by parliament – Maciej Berek - was prevented from taking his seat amid scuffles outside the Tribunal in Warsaw. On Saturday, riot police reinforced security measures around the court in central Warsaw. ‘There is no other way,’ says Tusk Tusk, who has spent much of his time as Prime Minister trying to unstitch the PiS changes to the judiciary, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law. “This process is difficult, at times even painful, ‌and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he said on X Saturday. In a televised speech Tusk said that “shouting, lies, and brawling cannot be the source of law in Poland, and they never will be.” He insisted the Tribunal “will function as it should. Also, independently of me and in line with the constitution.” Analysts say the crisis deepened when parliament approved the nomination of Berek, a close ally of Tusk. It “contradicts the government’s pledge to depoliticise the Tribunal,” wrote Alberto Allemano, a professor of law at the HEC Paris Business School. “The Friday suspension of the Tribunal’s president and vice-president, ordered by one judge and accompanied by a police presence outside the building, is not in itself a “coup”: the stated aim is to restore a lawfully functioning court. But restoring the rule of law must itself be done lawfully,” Allemano wrote on X. At the same time, “If the Polish government is trying to repair an institution captured under PiS, its opposition is striving to retain some control through illegal means,” he added. The US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose warned on Friday night that “thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.” “I hope everyone involved—government officials, law enforcement, and demonstrators alike, to take a deep breath, and don’t take any action that could provoke violence or further escalation,” Rose said on X. But it’s unclear how the standoff between Tusk and Nawrocki can be resolved. Neither seems ready to compromise at a time when Poland faces growing security threats – with the war across the border in Ukraine, and sabotage attacks inside Poland that Tusk has attributed to Russia. Tusk said Saturday of his opponents that it was “no coincidence that they find support among pro-Russian forces around the world.” Fresh elections are due next year, with Poland’s constitutional order and its political direction – towards or away from deeper integration with Europe – high on the agenda.

articles.title: 12 killed, more than 60 injured in Halloween weekend shootings across seven states
articles.summary: One person was killed and eight others were wounded in a mass shooting just outside Legion Field after the annual ‘Magic City Classic’ football game on Saturday night, police in Birmingham, Ala., said.
articles.body: At least 12 people were killed and more than 60 were injured in shootings across seven states overnight, including three separate incidents in a Dallas arts district where four people died. In Dallas’ Deep Ellum neighborhood, three shootings left at least four dead and 15 injuries, Dallas Police Chief Daniel C. Comeaux said. A preliminary assessment indicated the shootings were not connected, he said. Some victims took themselves to hospitals, and casualty numbers could change, Comeaux said at a news conference. A witness described chaos interrupting a night of Halloween revelry. “Right after one shooting, you would hear another shooting, and you would see all the police officers take off running to the next scene,” Jessica Gamboa told NBC News. “It was a scary and unbelievable night.” In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in a shooting outside Legion Field after Saturday night’s Magic City Classic football game. Birmingham Police Chief Michael Pickett said most spectators and families had left the stadium grounds, but the gunfire erupted nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue. He said he was “very grateful that more people weren’t injured.” The circumstances remained unclear. One person was detained and taken to police headquarters for questioning, and “multiple weapons” were found and secured, a police spokesperson said. The annual game between Alabama State and Alabama A&M, historically Black universities and archrivals, has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game. Two University of Colorado-Boulder students were shot, one fatally, at a house party in Boulder more than an hour after police responded to the house to address a noise complaint, police said. Police left the scene after shutting down the party shortly after 10 p.m., taking one person on a hold because they were extremely intoxicated. Another call came in around 11:30 p.m. to report a shooting, Boulder Police Chief Stephen Redfearn said at a news conference. Two 19-year-olds were found with gunshot wounds at the home and one died after being transported to the hospital, Redfearn said. Two people of interest are being sought in connection to the homicide. In Jacksonville, Florida, a 17-year-old girl and a 20-year-old man were fatally shot in a pair of unrelated shootings at Halloween parties that left 11 others with injuries. The girl was an unintended victim in a crowd waiting to enter a party around 1:45 a.m., police said. Investigators believe there were two gunmen. The man was at a house party when a fatal fight broke out, police said. He died at a hospital. In Bloomington, Illinois, a 19-year-old woman died and seven were injured in a shooting near Illinois Wesleyan University. Police have not identified her, pending notification of her family. In Jackson, Mississippi, a man and a woman were fatally shot and two others were injured at a nightclub, police said. One man was killed and several others were injured in shooting before 2 a.m., according to local police. Six people were also injured, none fatally, in a shooting near the University of Delaware in Newark, Delaware. Police are investigating.

articles.title: Tensions flare in South China Sea: Taiwan accuses China of harassing coast guard
articles.summary: Taiwan's coast guard has accused China of harassing its vessels and attempting to assert \"fictional jurisdiction\" in the South China Sea and waters east
articles.body: Taiwan's coast guard has accused China of harassing its vessels and attempting to assert "fictional jurisdiction" in the South China Sea and waters east of the island, as tensions between the two sides continue to escalate.The latest confrontation came early on Saturday when a Chinese coast guard vessel entered restricted waters near the Pratas Islands, a Taiwan-administered coral island strategically located in the northern part of the South China Sea. Taiwan's coast guard said one of its vessels confronted the Chinese ship and ordered it to leave. At the height of the standoff, the two vessels came within one nautical mile (1.9 kilometres) of each other.Taiwan's coast guard said the incident marked the 13th Chinese intrusion near the Pratas Islands this year, involving 16 vessels. It urged Beijing "to immediately cease these pointless acts of harassment".Separately, China announced that it had deployed a group of coast guard vessels for a "routine law enforcement patrol" in waters east of Taiwan. Two Chinese ships were involved in the operation, prompting Taipei to send its own vessels to monitor their movements.Taiwan accused China of using radio communications to harass ships and expand its presence in the region. It said Beijing's actions violated international law and undermined regional peace and stability, adding that China had no jurisdiction over Taiwan's waters. Beijing, however, maintains that the waters it patrols fall under its jurisdiction.Taipei has grown increasingly concerned about China's regular coast guard patrols along its eastern coast, which have intensified since June. Taiwanese officials believe the operations could be part of preparations for a potential maritime blockade, using a combination of military, paramilitary and civilian vessels to restrict access to the island. The eastern coastline is particularly important to Taiwan as a potential route for supplies from allies during a conflict.The developments come amid wider concerns over Beijing's growing military and maritime activity around Taiwan. articles.summary: The Roman coin hoard on Gotland features five emperors and four empresses from the second century A.D., but two coins may be ancient fakes from Ukraine.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Sweden recently made an unusual discovery. They found 45 ancient Roman silver coins, including two believed to be counterfeits. The discovery was announced by the Swedish Armed Forces earlier this fall. The coins were unearthed during archaeological excavations ahead of an expansion of Sweden's Gotland Regiment military base, according to officials. MYSTERIOUS FIND BENEATH FIELD LEADS MAN TO MASSIVE TREASURE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES "During one of the excavations, an unusual find was made — a silver treasure with Roman coins from the second century A.D.," the Swedish Armed Forces said in a translated statement. The discovery came as archaeologists were wrapping up an excavation of a farmhouse foundation dating to the Migration Period, which spanned roughly the fifth and sixth centuries A.D. The archaeologists were making "one final sweep with the metal detector" before the discovery, according to officials. "Then an insistent beeping indicated that something was in the ground near one of the foundation stones," the statement said. "They carefully dug a small silver coin out of the soil — and more finds would follow." RARE COIN BEARING FACE OF KING WITH INFAMOUS NICKNAME UNEARTHED AFTER 1,000 YEARS When archaeologists brushed off the coin, they discovered a stamped portrait of Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius, who ruled from 138 to 161 A.D. "The metal detector's persistent beeping indicated that more objects were hidden near the same foundation stone," officials said. "Before the workday was over, archaeologists had counted 45 coins and a gold finger ring. All the coins are Roman, minted during the second century for five emperors and four empresses." The coins were identified by Lennart Lind, a Swedish expert on Roman coins. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER SPRAWLING ROMAN ESTATE BURIED FOR CENTURIES BENEATH FARMLAND The coins feature five Roman emperors — Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius and Commodus — as well as four empresses: Vibia Sabina, Faustina I, Faustina II and Lucilla, according to officials. Experts believe the coins arrived on Gotland during the fourth century and were used in trade for generations before being buried alongside the gold ring around 450 A.D. "It looks like it was slowly abandoned, and some of the people might even have come back to this place to get more things back to a new settlement." Two of the coins, however, were ancient counterfeits that may have originated in what is now Ukraine, according to archaeologists. Widerström told Fox News Digital the silver coins were largely what archaeologists would expect to uncover at such a site, but the gold ring was unusual. articles.title: Burnham ‘open’ to UK slavery apology, but not reparations: Why now?
articles.summary: The UK PM’s statement comes as Commonwealth nations meet in Antigua and Barbuda.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his country is open to apologising for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade but ruled out reparations, which campaigners have for years called for.

Burnham wrote in an opinion article in The Guardian on Friday that Britain would also work on debt restructuring for the poorest countries, marking an historic turn in London’s stance.

The move comes ahead of a four-day summit starting Sunday of the 50-plus Commonwealth nations formerly colonised by Britain. The UK’s King Charles, who arrived in the Caribbean last week, is hosting the leaders in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnham wrote, in what amounted to a personal apology.

Caribbean nations that have more forcefully demanded reparations in recent years said they expect more from Britain, while opposition Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised Burnham’s move as “navel-gazing”.

Transatlantic slavery lasted between the 16th and 19th centuries and saw some 12 million enslaved Africans torn from their homes and forcibly transported on ships to the Americas with the help of local warlords. Enslaved people were sold on plantations and as domestic workers, and their labour produced goods that built wealth in Europe.

Britain and Portugal accounted for about 70 percent of all Africans exported to the Americas, while France, Spain and the Netherlands also traded in significant numbers of enslaved people. Britain alone transported 3.1 million Africans to British colonies in the Caribbean, the Americas and other countries, according to its national archives. Only 2.7 million arrived, as many perished in treacherous sea journeys.

British abolitionists began campaigning against slavery in 1787, particularly in cities like Manchester. In 1807, Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act, essentially banning new enslavement. More than three decades later, in 1834, Britain banned slavery in its entirety, although the practice continued for several years.

Amid calls for accountability in 2006, then-Prime Minister Tony Blair expressed “deep sorrow” for Britain’s role in the slave trade, but fell short of apologising or speaking about reparations.

Burnham’s apology came during Britain’s Black History Month and as the Commonwealth is meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

In his article, the British prime minister said London wants to keep diplomatic and trade ties with its Commonwealth allies.

“In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests,” he wrote, adding that Britain “can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration”.

Britain will allow the most vulnerable countries to repay their debts over a longer period, he added, with former Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, who spearheaded the UK’s 1991 initiative to reduce debt for poorer countries, leading the charge.

What is the debate regarding apologies and reparations?

Since 2013, the Caribbean Community and Common Market (CARICOM) has called on Western countries involved to acknowledge their role and institute monetary reparations for slavery.

In recent years, those calls have grown louder, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley.

Ghana, where around 10-15 percent of enslaved people were transferred from, has also played a major role and pushed a historic resolution at the United Nations in March that saw 123 countries vote to declare trafficking of enslaved Africans the gravest crime against humanity. All European nations abstained while the United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the measure.

Campaigners argue that there is a legal and moral case for financial payment and debt cancellations for the centuries of damage caused by enslavement. Those damages, they say, are evident in the structural inequalities that continue to plague countries where human capital was stolen from and those in the Caribbean that faced genocides after Europeans arrived.

They also point to the loss of lives, the erasure of cultures, the looting of artefacts in the colonial era that followed, and ongoing economic disparities and development challenges that see those nations struggle to access international financial institutions.

In June, Mottley announced a 19-point manifesto at a conference in Ghana, as Caribbean and African countries increasingly align to more strongly push their case. It called for a “full and formal apology”, monetary compensation from nations, but also institutions, including corporations and churches. It also called for technology transfer, education and healthcare funding, debt relief and economic development. The plan revised an earlier CARICOM 10-point plan.

“We live in a world today where people call out people for everything, for misogyny, for sexual assault, for all kinds of behaviour. But yet we have not found the moral courage to state unanimously across humanity that this grave crime against humanity that persisted for centuries ought to be declared so by all,” Mottley said at the conference.

Why are European nations not keen on reparations?

European nations, including Britain, argue that those crimes were committed long ago and that, as such, their people should not pay for them. Some also point to the role of local African chiefs who worked with the Europeans to kidnap and enslave people.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” Burnham wrote in The Guardian.

Instead, he said, the UK was “offering a structured dialogue” with those affected and debt restructuring.

France recognised slavery as a crime against humanity in 2001. In May, French President Emmanuel Macron said Paris should look into reparations, but did not make clear proposals.

In 2022, the Netherlands apologised for its role.

The Church of England, whose clergy also owned enslaved people, set up a fund of 100 million British pounds ($134mn) to cater to affected communities and to conduct further research into slavery’s legacies.

In a statement, Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister Philip J Pierre, who currently chairs CARICOM, said the organisation rejects the argument that Britain of today cannot be held responsible for slavery.

“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions — and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said. Without repair, PM Burnham’s apology was “incomplete”, he added.

Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama said he welcomed Burnham’s statement with “caution” and reiterated the need for a formal apology, targeted investments in several sectors, and an international commitment to “dismantle systemic racism and Afrophobia”.

Denis O’Brien, founder of the advocacy group The Repair Campaign, also said London “must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now”.

The UK’s opposition Conservative Party leader Badenoch kicked against the move entirely in a post on X, and asked whether the descendants of African rulers involved would also be asked for reparations.

“There is no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born,” she said.

“Labour are already spending too much on Britain’s welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare.”

Meanwhile, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, which endorses compensation, welcomed Burnham’s steps but said action was still “lacking”.

articles.title: Serbia arrests police chief over abuse of office allegations
articles.summary: Belgrade’s chief prosecutor says arrest of Marko Kricak ‘has no link’ to elections that saw Aleksandar Vucic step down.
articles.body:
Serbian authorities have arrested the head of the country’s criminal police directorate on suspicion of abuse of office, while denying there are any links to elections held a week ago.

Marko Kricak, 42, was arrested on Sunday along with the police commander in charge of fighting organised crime, Bosko Sekulovic, Belgrade’s chief prosecutor said.

Prosecutor Nenad Stefanovic said the two were suspected of abusing their offices and failing to uphold their duties, “thus causing prejudice and serious harm to the rights of Belgrade’s former police chief”, Veselin Milic.

The allegations surfaced in an investigation into the murder of a suspected criminal underworld figure in a Belgrade restaurant in May.

Milic, who was arrested days after the murder for failing to report the crime and helping the perpetrator, began legal action while in custody against Kricak and Sekulovic, accusing them of giving prosecutors incomplete and false evidence.

Kricak is seen as a loyalist to defeated President Aleksandar Vucic. The police chief was accused by student groups of “brutality” in the police response to demonstrations that helped bring down Vucic’s ruling right-wing party.

Last week they demanded his removal, along with that of several other police and intelligence chiefs, as part of sweeping reforms.

However, the prosecutor’s office did not provide any link between Kricak’s arrest and the students’ demands.

“This arrest has no link with … the result of the legislative elections,” Stefanovic told journalists.

The Student List, a student-backed movement, won a historic victory on October 25 in snap elections called by Vucic after nearly two years of protests, ending 14 years of rule by his Serbian Progressive Party.

The arrests come as Serbia marks two years since the Novi Sad railway station disaster.

On Sunday, thousands gathered in Novi Sad to mark the day that a concrete canopy collapsed at the city’s newly renovated railway station, killing 16 people.

The crowd observed 16 minutes of silence, one for each victim, as the students marched silently through the rain carrying wreaths.

“It’s hard to go back to the place where it all happened,” Dijana Hrka, whose 27-year-old son Stefan was killed, told the AFP news agency. “I believe justice will be served.”

In a statement, students said “tragedy” was not enough to describe what happened.

“Tragedy describes an accident,” they said. “But behind that word, one can cleverly conceal the word we are all looking for: responsibility.”

The collapse set off Serbia’s biggest protests since the fall of former President Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. Prime Minister Milos Vucevic resigned in January 2025, and Vucic stepped down as president in September to lead his party’s list, pardoning students and activists prosecuted over the protests.

articles.title: Henry Nowak: Southampton student’s family on police footage
articles.summary: His family describe the night police told them of his death, and watching him being handcuffed.
articles.body:
The family of Henry Nowak have said the trauma of learning he had been murdered was made worse by watching police footage of officers handcuffing him as he lay dying.

They told ITV their "world has changed twice", first when they were told he had died, and again when they watched the body-worn camera video.

His killer, Vickrum Digwa, falsely told police Henry had racially abused him , and officers handcuffed the student as he repeatedly said he had been stabbed.

His father Mark, stepmother Katie, mother Lucy and sister Olivia were speaking to ITV for the documentary Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder , led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk, which will look at "any missed opportunities to intervene".

Henry, 18, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.

He was stabbed five times as he walked home from a night out with friends from his football team in Southampton on 3 December 2025.

It took officers another 24 hours to identify Henry's body and tell his family.

"I jumped out of bed and I saw the police car on our driveway," said Katie.

"One of the police officers was holding his hat in his hand, and I just knew straight away that something horrific had happened."

She said Mark fell to his knees when he heard the news.

"He let out a cry that I'll never forget," she said.

"I just remember saying 'it's Henry' and breaking down in tears," Mark said. "It's just unbelievable pain."

Officers went to Lucy's home at the same time.

"We got that dreaded knock on the door at one o'clock in the morning," she said.

"They said to me, 'Do you have a son called Henry?… There's been an altercation. And unfortunately, your son has passed away'.

"No words, no words can explain that feeling."

Olivia said she rang her father after hearing the news. "I just remember this scream. It was awful. He screamed 'My boy, my boy'," she said.

She now keeps some of Henry's T-shirts on his bed and told ITV they still smell of him and give her comfort.

But Lucy said she could no longer enter his bedroom because of the memories it holds.

Coats now hang over the bedroom door so she does not have to look at it as she passes.

The murder caused widespread political outrage when the footage emerged.

In the video, Henry can be heard repeatedly saying "I've been stabbed", to which an officer replies: "Don't think you have, mate."

It is also looking at whether race, religion or prejudice affected police decisions.

The watchdog said it expected its investigation to conclude early next year.

"In the last year, our world has changed twice," Katie said.

"The first time was the night that we were told that Henry had died. And the second time was when we watched that video."

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

Chalk said: "Serious questions have been raised about whether agencies and organisations failed to act on complaints about Digwa's violent and erratic behaviour.

"My review will follow the evidence without fear or favour. It will also examine how public authorities treated the Nowak family at a time of unimaginable pain."

articles.title: Al Jazeera Balkans relaunches in new digital-first format
articles.summary: AJB’s return is a ‘reaffirmation’ of the network’s mission to go where the story matters, says its digital director.
articles.body:
Al Jazeera Balkans has officially returned to audiences across the Balkans region, opening a new chapter in its journalism with a digital-first platform.

The launch on Sunday, November 1, marks an evolution of Al Jazeera Balkans (AJB) , building on the editorial credibility, regional expertise and distinctive voice that established the brand across the region, while reimagining its journalism for a new generation of digital audiences.

AJB first launched in 2011 , before the channel shut down in 2025.

In the weeks leading up to the official relaunch, AJB began publishing across its social media platforms, reconnecting with audiences through coverage of major regional developments, including elections in Serbia and protests in Albania .

During this period, its content generated close to 100 million views across social media.

Al Jazeera’s Director of Digital News Content and Languages Jamal Elshayyal hailed the digital relaunch as a reaffirmation of the network’s values.

“The Balkans is a region whose stories, struggles and suffering have too often been seen only when they become impossible for the world to ignore. Yet behind the headlines are societies in transformation, communities shaped by extraordinary resilience, and people asking to be heard,” Elshayyal said.

“The launch of Al Jazeera Balkans in this new digital form is a reaffirmation of what has always been at the heart of Al Jazeera: going where the story matters, listening to the voice of the voiceless, and giving people the space to tell their own stories.

“At a moment when the region needs greater attention and deeper understanding, we want Al Jazeera Balkans to be a window from the Balkans to the world, and from the world back to the Balkans.”

At the heart of the new AJB is an expanded editorial vision for the entire region.

Alongside Al Jazeera’s coverage of major global developments, audiences can now access a dedicated “ Balkans ” section on the website and follow news from individual countries across the region, including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, North Macedonia and others.

AJB is strengthening its presence across social media, with short-form videos and explainers that will quickly give audiences key information and context around major regional and global developments, as well as the introduction of podcasts.

AJB will also extend its journalism beyond the geographical borders of the Balkans. Particular attention will be given to the Balkan diaspora, including significant communities in Germany, the United States and other relevant countries.

For this new digital-first chapter, audiences can follow Al Jazeera Balkans across Instagram , Facebook , TikTok, YouTube, X , Threads and other social media platforms, as well as on its digital portal, balkans.aljazeera.net .

articles.title: Russia detains minor over alleged Moscow attack plot after US warning
articles.summary: Russian authorities say a US tip-off helped them identify teenager suspected of planning attack at a Moscow park.
articles.body:
Russian authorities have detained a teenager suspected of planning an attack at a popular Moscow park after receiving a warning from the United States, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency, citing the Federal Security Service (FSB).

The FSB said the suspect, a Russian citizen, posted photos on TikTok wearing a balaclava and tactical clothing and holding what appeared to be an automatic weapon, Interfax reported on Sunday.

The suspect, who has not been identified, also reportedly shared photos taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in southern Moscow with the caption: “I found a place.”

The FSB said a search of the suspect’s home uncovered the clothing and accessories seen in the photos, Interfax reported. The security service also said that the teen’s phone showed searches related to terrorist attacks and mass killings, as well as a subscription to a neo-Nazi Telegram channel.

The detention came after the US embassy in Moscow issued a security alert on Saturday warning of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a popular palace and park complex.

The embassy urged people to avoid the area and said the US government was coordinating with Russian authorities on a response.

The park was temporarily closed on Saturday following the warning.

“We are grateful to the American side for providing the information,” the FSB said in its statement.

Russia’s Investigative Committee is now considering what legal action to take against the suspect, the FSB said.

The US has previously warned Russia about potential attacks, including in March 2024, weeks before an attack on a Moscow concert hall by an affiliate of the ISIL group that killed more than 140 people.

The latest warning comes despite longstanding tensions between Washington and Moscow over Russia’s war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Israel’s president says parties need to engage with ‘open heart’ to avoid fresh election
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged the country’s political parties to enter negotiations on forming a new government with an “open heart,” as he prepares to consult with factions on a path forward after an uncertain election result.
articles.body: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged the country’s political parties to enter negotiations on forming a new government with an “open heart,” as he prepares to consult with factions on a path forward after an uncertain election result. Last week’s elections saw Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc denied a majority, with the parties in his ruling coalition claiming 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset. Parties in the bloc aligned with Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, leaving neither man with an obvious path to forming a government. The balance of power is held by parties representing Israel’s minority Arab community, which nearly doubled its representation in Israel’s parliament with 19 seats. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot had ruled out working with them prior to the vote. Netanyahu has since continued to attack the Arab parties, accusing them of holding stances on Gaza and the West Bank he considers unacceptable. Eisenkot, however, has indicated he is open to working with anyone who agrees to four conditions on Israeli sovereignty and opposition to Hamas, potentially opening a path to a deal that could propel him to power and avoid fresh elections. While Netanyahu is the leader of the single largest party, it is up to Herzog — largely a ceremonial figure — to decide who has the first shot at forming a government. He will hold initial consultations with party officials on Wednesday, beginning a delicate process that could last weeks. “I hope the representatives will come with an open mind, and today I add: with an open heart,” Herzog said in a statement Sunday. “Come to listen and to be heard, to share ideas, and to find creative solutions to prevent another round of elections.” Netanyahu, who is set to remain in his post as a caretaker until a new government can be formed, has claimed Arab parties used foreign backing to “steal” the elections, without providing evidence. Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet has said it is investigating possible foreign interference in the election but that the probe was not intended to “cast aspersions” on any specific group. Arab party leaders have strongly denied any wrongdoing, while Herzog pushed party leaders to accept the election result. “During an election campaign, candidates naturally and predictably climb to lofty positions,” Herzog said in his statement. “But the elections are over. The election results are a fact. They are a reality. And now is the time to call on all our leaders to stop climbing and face this reality.” The four conditions Eisenkot set out for prospective partners include recognizing Israel as a Jewish state, committing to the values of its independence, accepting mandatory military service for all Israeli citizens and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization. “Every Knesset member who is willing to sign on to these principles is a potential partner on the path to establishing a new and better government for Israel,” he said in a statement on Saturday. “The door to the government we will form will be open to every public representative who accepts these principles and is ready to rise to the occasion.” Netanyahu, meanwhile, said Sunday that it was “forbidden” to form a government with Mansour Abbas, head of Arab-led party Ra’am. He said on X that Abbas wants to establish a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, and evacuate Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, citing an old Ra’am policy platform. During the campaign, Netanyahu’s Likud party repeatedly alleged that Eisenkot would usher the Arab parties into power. In one of several AI-generated videos posted by Netanyahu, Eisenkot was portrayed astride a wooden Trojan horse, with Abbas and left-wing politician Yair Golan inside. Abbas said Friday that he was coordinating with other Arab leaders on “the prospects for forming a government to replace the one led by Netanyahu.” Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc contains a broad array of ideologies and views on the issue, ranging from Golan, who has publicly advocated for a deal with the Arab parties, to Avigdor Lieberman of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, who continues to oppose working with them. With that much friction, a stalemate and more elections remain a real possibility. Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News that Israel still appears stuck, adding that Eisenkot’s conditions for the Arab parties are effectively asking them to “forsake their identity.” “I don’t think we will see the opposition led by Eisenkot forming a government in Israel,” he said. “So what we have now is a deadlock.” For the major Israeli parties, it is a choice “between Israel as a democratic state or Israel as a Zionist exclusive society,” he said. But Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Program at U.K. think tank Chatham House, sees flexibility that could yield a breakthrough. Parties “make all these promises before the election, and it is obvious that you break at least some of them after the election,” he said.

articles.title: Thousands of jobs at Virgin Media O2 to be cut
articles.summary: The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be axed but it will likely be a sizeable chunk of its workforce, the BBC understands.
articles.body:
Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff face redundancy risk as the telecoms firm looks to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition.

The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000 workforce, the BBC understands.

VMO2 has billions of debt on its balance sheet and is tackling competition from both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, a move which VMO2 has firmly opposed.

VMO2 declined to comment. The Prospect union, which represents VMO2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling".

Deputy general secretary Noel McClean said it is "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected".

The majority of the affected staff will be in non-customer facing roles and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told.

VMO2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts that were first reported by Sky News.

As of 30 June, VMO2's total debt stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts.

Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear, and YouFibre.

VMO2's had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by VMO2's owners.

However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal , with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from VMO2.

At the time, VMO2 called the BT takeover a "stitch-up", which allowed its rival "tighten its grip" over the market.

BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover.

On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported VMO2 was close to agreeing a deal to use its rival's fibre broadband network.

VMO2 was minded to go ahead with the plans after halting upgrades and expansion of its own infrastructure to ease concerns over its debt pile, the paper reported.

The BBC has been told the deal is very close and that VMO2 is highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday.

articles.title: Russia’s security service detains a teenager planning a ‘terror attack’ after a US tip-off
articles.summary: A suspect allegedly planning a terror attack on a major Moscow museum was arrested by Russian authorities after a tip-off from the United States, Russia’s security agency FSB announced on Sunday.
articles.body: A suspect allegedly planning a terror attack on a major Moscow museum was arrested by Russian authorities after a tip-off from the United States, Russia’s security agency FSB announced on Sunday. The FSB said information shared with Russia by US law enforcement led to the arrest of the Russian citizen who is a minor. The agency said it was “grateful to the US side for the information provided.” The arrest came after the US Embassy in Moscow issued a security alert on Saturday, warning it was “aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow. CNN contacted the museum after the alert was issued and was told the institution was not aware of any warnings. However, several events scheduled to take place at the venue were later canceled and security measures were put in place, according to Russian state media. The unnamed suspect was detained after posting images on TikTok of himself wearing tactical clothing and an “object resembling an automatic weapon” and sharing photos taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: “I found a place,” according to the FSB. The FSB said the teenager subscribed to a neo-Nazi channel on Telegram and made “significant number of search queries regarding past terrorist acts, mass murders, and other violent acts.” It said airsoft weapons were found at the suspect’s home. It is not unusual for the US to share security warnings with other countries — the State Department has a long-standing “duty to warn” policy and is obligated to let US expat communities know of any threats. The alert issued on Saturday said the US government was “coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response.” However, Russia has not always received US warnings with thanks. In March 2024, during the Biden administration era, the US embassy in Moscow warned that ISIS militants were determined to target Russia, specifically saying there were “imminent plans to target large gatherings in Moscow,” including at concerts. Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed that warning as a provocation. Days later, assailants stormed Moscow’s Crocus City Hall venue and killed more than 140 people. ISIS claimed responsibility for the attack. Putin’s reaction was different in 2017, during US President Donald Trump’s first presidency, when the US warned Moscow about a planned terror attack at the Kazan Cathedral in St Petersburg. According to a Kremlin statement, Putin personally thanked Trump for the information, saying it was enough to locate and detain the suspects. The latest warning and the FSB’s public statement thanking the US, comes at a time of an increased scrutiny of the Trump administration’s relationship with Russia. Trump has made significant concessions to Russia on sanctions in recent weeks, which have triggered criticism on both sides of the aisle in Washington and driven a wedge between the US and its Western allies.

articles.title: Bhutan dedicates Buddhist stupa to PM Modi; Rijiju calls it ‘huge honour’ for India
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bhutan's King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck has dedicated a sacred Buddhist stupa to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, recognising his
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bhutan's King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck has dedicated a sacred Buddhist stupa to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, recognising his contribution to strengthening friendship between the two countries. The dedication of Stupa number 76 took place during a ceremony to raise and consecrate 108 stupas in Gelephu Mindfulness City on Sunday.According to news agency ANI, Union minority affairs minister Kiren Rijiju represented India at the ceremony and expressed gratitude to Bhutan for the gesture, describing it as a "huge honour for India". He also conveyed gratitude on behalf of Prime Minister Modi to the Bhutanese King.In a post on X, Rijiju said, "It's a huge honour for India that very sacred stupa 76 is dedicated to Hon'ble PM Narendra Modi ji for his outstanding vision and commitment to friendship between India and Bhutan. On the auspicious occasion of Lhabab Duchen, joined the sacred ceremony in Gelephu Mindfulness City, Bhutan, marking the raising and consecration of 108 stupas, accompanied by the blowing of Dungchens."He further said, "Paid my respects and offered prayers in the presence of His Majesty the King of Bhutan, Her Majesty the Gyaltsuen, H E Dasho Tshering Tobgay, Prime Minister of Bhutan & the people of Bhutan. A deeply meaningful spiritual occasion, reflecting Bhutan’s rich Buddhist heritage and the enduring bonds of friendship between our two nations."Stupas are sacred Buddhist structures associated with the teachings and life of Gautama Buddha. Traditionally, they were built to preserve the relics of the Buddha and other revered Buddhist figures, including their ashes and remains. Over time, they became important places of worship, meditation and religious devotion.The 108 stupas in Bhutan are known as Jangchub Chortens, or Stupas of Enlightenment. The number 108 holds special significance in Buddhist traditions and is associated with religious practices, including the use of 108 beads in prayer malas. The structures are intended to promote peace, harmony and spiritual well-being.Rijiju is visiting Bhutan from October 31 to November 2. Earlier on Sunday, Rijiju met Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay in Gelephu. The two leaders discussed strengthening the India-Bhutan partnership and exploring the potential of the Gelephu Mindfulness City project.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy will reappear in court - but will her case be retried?
articles.summary: The Massachusetts mother, accused of murdering her three children, is expected back in court as she awaits a decision on whether her case will be retried.
articles.body:
Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, will return to a Massachusetts court on Monday as lawyers debate retrying the case.

Her defence team and Massachusetts prosecutors are expected to discuss how to move forward, with both parties seeking different outcomes.

Last week, in response to a defence request to dismiss the trial, prosecutors offered their clearest hint yet that they are seeking a new trial before a different jury. "The Commonwealth [Massachusetts] should be permitted to continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy," her three children, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors could also reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.

The 36-year-old has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.

What happened when Clancy was last in court?

A jury first heard Clancy's case in August 2026, but failed to reach a unanimous agreement on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law.

A judge declared a mistrial in early September.

At a court appearance later that month, Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued the judge should dismiss her case. Meanwhile, prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt.

But the hours-long back-and-forth ultimately didn't lead to a clearer answer about what might come next for Clancy - a dismissal of charges, retrial of the same charges, or retrial of lesser charges. These discussions will resume on Monday.

Judge William Sullivan seemed confident the case would be retried, saying in September he wanted to "get this thing moving".

He asked both sides to prepare to discuss possible trial dates at the November hearing.

Reddington said he would be unable to go to trial until at least June 2027 if the case was retried.

District Attorney Timothy Cruz said at the time that prosecutors had not yet decided whether to retry Clancy.

"We're doing our due diligence; we're going to continue doing that," he said. "We're going to do what we can for the children. That's what this case is about."

Fundamentally, Clancy's legal team - with Reddington at the helm - is pushing for the charges to be dismissed or dropped. They've explored a variety of legal avenues.

In September, he asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts provision that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not present enough evidence at trial.

Judge Sullivan will hear arguments on several motions on Monday, but Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and mental health law expert, told the BBC that the hearing will likely focus on a narrow point: was this an instance of a routine deadlocked-jury mistrial - in which the jury genuinely could not agree - or was this an improperly terminated trial?

She said Reddington may argue that a retrial could violate Clancy's Constitutional protection against double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.

But legal experts agree that outcome is unlikely.

"The public attention that's been put on this trial and the need to have some conclusion in the near future, I think that the judge is going to say that this mistrial was appropriate, was legally accurate, and that they need to now look to set a date for a retrial," Cucolo said.

While the state's legal team has not explicitly said they will pursue a retrial, Cruz and the prosecutors who argued the case have consistently said they want justice for Clancy's children.

Last week, prosecutors asked Judge Sullivan to reject the motion to dismiss charges against Clancy on the grounds of double jeopardy.

They argue mistrial procedures were properly followed by the court, and thus they have a right to seek justice again on behalf of the children.

"Because a mistrial was properly declared due to the manifest necessity of a deadlocked jury, the defendant's motion to dismiss should be denied," prosecutors wrote in the motion.

Judge Sullivan could make a determination over whether the case can proceed on Monday or he could rule later in writing, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.

And how the District Attorney's office wants to proceed could be determined ahead of Monday's hearing, during it or even days after, she said.

"The three charges of first-degree murder are still pending; they are still hanging over Lindsay Clancy's head unless and until the DA announces otherwise," Hershon said.

Historically, Cruz, the district attorney, has made comments and announcements about the case at press conferences after court finishes. That could happen again this week, she predicted.

It is also likely, Hershon said, that Judge Sullivan pushes the lawyers on both sides to get a trial date on the calendar during Monday's hearing.

"It does not mean it's definitely going to be a jury trial, but [they will want to] put something in the books, hold those dates. It's a big chunk of time. It's four, five, six weeks of the court calendar; that's hard to fit in at the last minute," she said.

"I would anticipate they block off the time while they go through all these motions and the DA's office figures out what it wants to do."

articles.title: Hebron siege continues for 10th day as Israel threatens wider offensive
articles.summary: Hebron’s economic losses surpass $3.8m as Israeli forces demolish West Bank homes and close hundreds of businesses.
articles.body:
Israeli forces are maintaining their siege on Hebron for the 10th consecutive day, threatening to expand their offensive and forcing more Palestinian families from their homes.

The lockdown in the occupied West Bank city was enforced after an attack on October 23 near Hebron in which two Israeli soldiers were killed.

More than 3,300 Palestinians have since been displaced or affected, with homes destroyed and businesses shut, according to the local municipality.

Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera on Saturday that daily economic losses were estimated to exceed 12 million shekels ($3.8m), with more than $1.9m worth of damage to infrastructure, along with losses in the health and environmental sectors estimated at about $160,000.

He said Israeli forces have demolished 15 homes and other structures and forced 327 businesses to close. About 80,000 students have been unable to attend school for 10 days, he added.

The mayor said Hebron accounts for about 40 percent of the Palestinian economy and the siege amounts to “collective punishment”.

Palestinian families in and around the city fear the army could soon extend its attacks.

Israeli arrests of Palestinians in Hebron and other cities in the occupied West Bank continued on Sunday.

Israeli forces arrested 10 Palestinian teachers in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron and seized their vehicle, reported the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

Video shared by Palestinian media and verified by Al Jazeera showed the Israeli military raiding a school run by the United Nations in the Shufat refugee camp in occupied East Jerusalem.

The United Nations humanitarian office, OCHA, said Israeli settlers carried out 397 attacks on Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in October, the highest monthly figure since monitoring began in 2006, Wafa said.

Between October 20 and 26, settler attacks targeted 49 Palestinian communities, mostly while Palestinians harvested olives on their land.

Nine children were among 57 Palestinians injured by settlers and Israeli forces: 34 by military gunfire and physical assaults and 23 in settler attacks.

Since the start of 2015, Israeli authorities have issued 9,518 demolition or stop-work notices against Palestinian property in the occupied West Bank, reported the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission. The Palestinian government commission added that 344 of those notices were given in the first nine months of this year.

articles.title: Texas firefighters rescue distressed raccoon after its head gets stuck in a hole in a tree
articles.summary: Video shows Austin firefighters using a catch pole to free a raccoon stuck in a tree hollow, but the animal's limp body raised immediate concerns.
articles.body: Raccoons are known for getting into all kinds of things while out scavenging for food. They will tip over garbage cans, rip open bags and even climb into an attic looking for food if they can find a way in. They will also use tree hollows for dens. Assuming, of course, that they fit into said tree hollow — which isn’t always the case, as firefighters in Austin, Texas, found out last week when a raccoon got its head stuck in a hole in a tree. A concerned neighbor called the Austin Fire Department to see if they could help the trash panda out. It wasn’t reported if the raccoon was after food or if it was in the market for a den when it became stuck in the tree. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS What was reported is that the firefighters answered the call, used a Jaws of Life-type tool, and freed the stuck animal from the hole in the tree. For everyone who has been concerned about the raccoon Austin firefighters recently rescued from a tree, we have good news!" the Austin Firefighter Association wrote. "Although the video may make it look like the raccoon is unconscious or has passed away when crews free him and lower him to the ground using a tool called a catch pole, we’re happy to report that he was alive and unharmed!" articles.title: Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland presents credentials in Hargeisa
articles.summary: Israel expands ties with the breakaway territory as Somalia challenges its motives and war intensifies in Yemen.
articles.body:
Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland has presented his credentials to the breakaway territory’s president, who formally accepted them at a ceremony in Hargeisa, where officials also laid the cornerstone for an Israeli embassy.

Israel’s Foreign Ministry announced the ceremonies on Sunday, saying they were held last week.

The move puts into practice an agreement reached on December 26, 2025, when Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise Somaliland, It declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but remains claimed by Mogadishu.

Describing it as a “historical day,” President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Cirro, said during the ceremony that it was the first time a Somaliland president had received the credentials of an ambassador from a UN member state recognising its independence.

Ambassador Michael Lotem said Israel’s recognition acknowledged what Somaliland had built over 35 years, rather than serving as a mere diplomatic formality.

Somaliland has governed itself for more than three decades, but remains without recognition from any other UN member state.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said in a statement on Sunday that the exchange of ambassadors fulfilled commitments made when relations were established.

Sa’ar visited Somaliland in January and the territory opened an embassy in West Jerusalem during Cirro’s visit to Israel in June.

At the ceremony in Hargeisa, Cirro stressed the broader importance of the relationship.

“Given our strategic position around the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, our cooperation carries important regional and international significance. Let me reaffirm that Somaliland approaches this relationship with genuine strategic commitment and a long-term perspective,” he said.

Somaliland lies across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen , near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the vital shipping passage between the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.

Fighting has intensified on the Yemeni side of the strait in recent weeks.

On October 9, United Nations envoy Hans Grundberg warned that Yemen had returned to full-scale war , with battles involving the Iran-aligned Houthi movement and forces of the internationally recognised government.

Israel has also acknowledged a security relationship that predates its diplomatic recognition.

During Cirro’s visit to Israel in June, Defence Minister Israel Katz said the two sides had cooperated on secret operations for years and wanted to expand their security ties.

Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud challenged Israel’s motives in an interview with Sky News this week, saying it was seeking access to the Red Sea rather than supporting Somaliland’s independence.

“Israel wants the Red Sea, that is the only reason,” he said.

Mohamud also alleged that Israel wants a naval base in the territory.

Somaliland officials have signalled openness to hosting an Israeli military base, but the territory’s president recently said no talks had been held.

Somalia condemned Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December as a violation of its sovereignty.

Israel’s move has also been condemned by the Arab League, African Union and Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

articles.summary: An avocado, egg white, tomato and spinach sandwich topped a Consumer Reports fast-food breakfast ranking, as Panera Bread beat out McDonald's and Starbucks.
articles.body: A popular restaurant chain grabbed four of the top 10 spots in a recent Consumer Reports fast-food breakfast item ranking — with its avocado, egg white and spinach sandwich winning first place and edging out items from major chains like McDonald’s and Starbucks. articles.title: Sullivan vows to honour Alaska race outcome, US judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit
articles.summary: Senator Sullivan’s pledge contrasts with the Trump administration’s effort to challenge Alaska’s election certification.
articles.body:
Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan has vowed to accept the election outcome days after the United States Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of the upcoming US Senate race there if the Republican incumbent loses.

“I’m going to accept the election results,” Sullivan, an ally of US President Donald Trump, told CNN on Sunday.

Sullivan’s promise comes just two days before the November 3 midterm election , which will determine control of the US Congress.

He said he was confident of winning, accusing his Democratic opponent Mary Peltola, who is attempting to unseat him, of cheating.

“My opponent and [Senate Minority Leader Chuck] Schumer and his aides are showing complete disrespect for Alaskans, complete disdain in recognising that they couldn’t run on their record, so they had to cheat. And now that that’s been exposed,” he said.

A New York Times report on Wednesday alleged that members of Peltola’s campaign helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J Sullivan Jr to run for the Senate seat as a spoiler candidate in an attempt to draw votes away from Senator Sullivan.

The report seems to have prompted the Trump administration’s renewed legal push to bar Alaska from certifying its election results, should Senator Sullivan lose.

On Sunday, US District Court Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the lawsuit, citing it as “infeasible” because many voters had already cast their ballots and the ballots have now been commingled to the point where the identity of each voter cannot be determined.

“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified “investigation” of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.

The second Sullivan is listed on the ballot as Daniel J Sullivan Jr, while the senator is listed as Dan S Sullivan and marked as a Republican incumbent.

Peltola has insisted she had nothing to do with recruiting the other Sullivan and has called attention to it a “distraction” from the main issues facing Alaskans — namely, high prices caused by US-Israel war on Iran. Her campaign has also denied involvement.

Before a rally on Friday, Peltola was asked whether someone on her campaign could have been involved in recruiting the other Sullivan. “I have no idea,” she told KTUU. “I honestly have no idea.”

Senator Sullivan doubted Peltola’s claims.

“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told the CNN news programme State of the Union. “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”

Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in the US Congress’s upper chamber.

Both candidates have spent the final days campaigning through Alaska’s vast landscape.

On Saturday night, Senator Sullivan handed out candy at a “trunk-or-treat” event at a recreation centre north of Anchorage, where he quipped his costume was “the real Dan Sullivan”.

articles.title: GCC makes GPS-tagged photos, videos of road milling mandatory
articles.summary: Greater Chennai Corporation mandates GPS-tagged photos/videos of road milling before relaying; 3-tier verification, online uploads, and strict action for violations.
articles.body: Chennai: Contractors relaying roads in Chennai can no longer simply lay a fresh layer of bitumen over an existing one. Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) has introduced a three-tier verification mechanism to ensure contractors remove existing bitumen layers before relaying roads.This comes amid rising demands from residents to ensure that contractors mill roads before relaying them, thereby preventing an increase in road height and consequent waterlogging of nearby homes.Under the new system, contractors must submit GPS-tagged photographs and videos documenting the milling process. Project management consultants and GCC officials will inspect the work, verify measurements and certify compliance, while a monitoring committee headed by senior officials will oversee quality and accountability. Photographs, videos and certifications will also be uploaded to the corporation’s website. The civic body warned of strict action against those who violate the guidelines.The move aims to prevent roads from progressively rising above adjoining properties with successive rounds of resurfacing, leaving house entrances and roadside drains at lower levels and increasing the risk of rainwater entering homes and commercial establishments.The civic body maintains 36,466 roads spanning 6,072.45km, including 488 bus route roads and 35,978 interior roads. Most are bituminous and are generally upgraded once every five years. According to GCC, edges inaccessible to cold milling machines must be cleared using other equipment or manual labour.The measures come as the corporation has invited tenders for road improvement works worth ₹130.19 crore in the first phase under the Chief Minister’s Integrated Urban Development Mission (CMIUDM). The state govt had announced ₹300 crore for road improvements across GCC limits under Rule 110. The initial detailed project report estimated the first phase at ₹154.16 crore.Corporation officials said several damaged roads, including stretches on Pillayar Koil Street, Udhyam Nagar, Kubera Nagar and Shalimar Garden, in Adyar and Perungudi zones, were laid on Sunday as part of the scheme.V Sandhya, vice-president of FOARA (Federation of Anna Nagar Residents Association), said: “The corporation should also include a member of Residents’ Welfare association to inspect the roads and check if they’re properly milled and re-laid.”She also said, “In many areas, the corporation officials lay roads without prior information to the residents, this also leaves a gap, as many tend to park vehicles outside their houses, the corporation should at least give a prior notice 15 days before re-laying a road.”“During checks by project management consultants (PMCs), if milling is found not to have been carried out, contractors will be directed to redo the work at their own cost. Payments for road relaying works will be withheld until mandatory milling is completed as per specifications. Repeated violations, negligence or non-compliance may lead to contract termination and blacklisting, as per applicable rules. Greater Chennai Corporation will not compromise on road quality and durability. articles.title: Condo wall damaged for a year, residents seek repairs before Diwali
articles.summary: Greater Noida West’s Nirala Greenshire residents seek repairs to a year-old broken boundary wall, garbage cleanup, streetlights and roads fixed before Diwali.
articles.body: Noida: Residents of Nirala Greenshire in Sector 2 of Greater Noida West have sought urgent repairs to a damaged boundary wall along the sector’s main road, which separates the complex from Nirala Trio. The wall, opposite towers G-11, G-12 and G-14, has remained damaged for nearly a year, raising safety and sanitation concerns. Residents also want nonfunctional streetlights and broken roads in the sector fixed before Diwali.According to residents, stray dogs have been gathering in the area. Overgrown bushes and inadequate lighting have also led to concerns over snakes and other wildlife. The lack of action from society management and GNIDA has turned the area potentially hazardous, they said.“The boundary wall has been damaged for nearly a year, posing safety and sanitation risks. Despite repeated complaints, there’s been no action taken. Residents want repairs before Diwali,” said Kapil Khare, a resident of the complex.The area around the damaged wall has also become a dumping ground. The current state of the spot has heightened safety concerns, particularly for children and senior citizens.“The problem has also affected approximately 100 designated parking spaces, which are exposed in the open in the absence of the boundary wall, causing considerable inconvenience to residents for an extended period. With Diwali approaching, the continued neglect of this issue is particularly concerning. Residents have urged Nirala management, GNIDA, and the police to intervene immediately and take appropriate action,” Khare added.With the festival approaching, residents are feeling an added sense of urgency. They have issued a set of demands to Nirala management and GNIDA, including prompt repair of the damaged boundary, removal of garbage and C&D waste near the wall, maintenance of overgrown bushes and provision of regular cleaning, installation of adequate street lighting to ensure safety during nighttime, and a transparent action plan with a definitive timeline for the completion of these tasks.Additionally, residents have also expressed concerns over nonfunctional streetlights in the area that plunge the roads into darkness on a nightly basis. Broken roads in desperate need of a revamp also add to the risk of accidents and dust pollution here.“With increased foot traffic, especially liquor shops nearby, we fear potential safety incidents if the situation remains unaddressed,” Khare said.When asked, Nirala estate management told TOI that the wall will be repaired soon.
